172.32.8.9 is outside 172.16.0.0/12 (which ends at 172.31.255.255), so it is a public address
Private ranges only exist in IPv6
Only 192.168.0.0/16 is private
explain: The /12 means the first 12 bits are fixed: 172.16 through 172.31. 172.32 is the first value outside it. Misreading private ranges is a classic triage mistake: it can make an external attacker look like an internal machine, or the reverse.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
question: Why are amplification attacks built on UDP services rather than TCP services?
options: UDP is always faster than TCP
UDP servers are usually unpatched
TCP traffic is encrypted, UDP is not
A single forged UDP datagram is a whole request, so the server replies to the forged address; TCP needs a handshake the spoofer cannot complete
explain: The handshake is TCP's accidental anti-spoofing check: the SYN-ACK goes to the real owner of the forged address and nothing further happens. UDP has no such step, so any server that answers a small UDP request with a big reply is a potential amplifier.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
question: In Wireshark you want only packets where a host tries to open a TCP connection. Which display filter is right?
options: tcp port 80
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0
tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0
tcp.flags.reset == 1
explain: A connection attempt is the first handshake segment: SYN set, ACK not set. `tcp port 80` and the `tcp[tcpflags]` expression are capture filter (pcap-filter) syntax, not display filter syntax, and the `tcp[tcpflags]` one would also match SYN-ACKs. Resets are a different event.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: Which data is the best candidate for interleaving?
options: A 40 GiB hash table read by threads on every node
Each worker thread's private 64 KiB scratch buffer
A 4 KiB counter page updated by all threads
explain: Interleave helps big structures with no natural owner by spreading their traffic over all controllers. Private buffers belong on their owner's node, and a single page is always on one node, so interleaving a 4 KiB object does nothing.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: The flash translation layer: a log plus a map
question: In the log-structured example, right after logical 100 and 101 are overwritten, why can't the FTL reuse physical pages 0 and 1 immediately?
options: They are still referenced by the map
Erasing works on whole blocks, and block 0 still holds live pages 2 and 3
Pages can only be reused after a power cycle
The FTL must wait for the host to send TRIM
explain: Pages 0 and 1 are dead, but the only way to make them writable is erasing block 0, which would destroy b1 and b2. Those live pages must be copied out first: that copy is garbage collection, and it is where write amplification comes from. TRIM (lesson 4) is the host saying which data is deleted; it cannot make a block with live pages erasable.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
question: Box A = (0, 0, 10, 10) and box B = (5, 0, 15, 10). What is their IoU?
explain: The intersection is 5 x 10 = 50. Each box is 100, so the union is 100 + 100 - 50 = 150, and IoU = 50 / 150 = 0.33. Half of each box overlaps, but IoU divides by the union, not by one box's area.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
question: Why does crossing-line counting tolerate the ID switch in the toy, while unique-ID counting does not?
options: The Kalman filter recovers the old ID
The new ID appeared after the car had already crossed, and only crossings are counted
Line counting ignores the detector
Unique-ID counting uses density maps
explain: The car crossed the line as ID 2 and was counted then. When it was re-detected as ID 3 it was already past the line, so it produced no new crossing. Unique-ID counting simply counts identities, so a broken track adds a phantom object. An ID switch right at the line can still cause a miss or double count.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
question: A topic has segment.bytes = 1 GiB, ingest of 5 MiB/s, tiered storage on, and local.retention.ms set to 1 minute. How much data can still be on the leader's local disk?
options: About 300 MiB, one minute of data
Zero, everything goes to S3 within a minute
At least the active segment, up to 1 GiB, because only rolled segments are copied and deleted
The full 7 days, because local retention is ignored
explain: Only rolled segments are copied to the remote tier, and local segments are not deleted until their copy succeeds. The active segment rolls only after 1 GiB (about 205 s at 5 MiB/s), so it always stays local. Retention works per segment, not per byte.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
question: Which panel earns the top-left corner of an incident dashboard for a user-facing service?
options: Per-pod CPU for all 50 pods
Garbage collection pause times
A heatmap of every internal RPC method's latency
SLO burn rate and error ratio for the user-facing endpoint
explain: The first question in any incident is whether users are hurt and how fast the budget is draining, which also decides whether to escalate. The other three are cause panels: useful at step three, useless as the first thing you see, and all three can look alarming during a perfectly healthy deploy.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
question: A team must extract fields from millions of scanned forms in a language their OCR engine handles poorly, and they do not need word-level boxes. Which approach does the Donut paper argue for?
options: An OCR-free model trained end to end, possibly pre-trained on synthetic pages in that language
LayoutLM with the existing OCR engine, since OCR errors do not matter
Tesseract with --psm 11
Rules over the OCR text
explain: Donut's motivation lists OCR cost, inflexibility of OCR across languages and document types, and OCR error propagation. Its SynthDoG generator exists precisely to pre-train in new languages and domains.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: SELinux: labels, types and the policy that decides
question: After a migration the site returns 403 and the audit log shows `avc: denied { read } ... scontext=...httpd_t... tcontext=...user_home_t... tclass=file` for files in /var/www/html. What is the best first fix?
options: Run audit2allow on the log and load every rule it prints
Relabel the files with restorecon so they get httpd_sys_content_t
chmod 777 the web root
setenforce 0, permanently
explain: The files kept the label of where they were created (a home directory). The policy is right; the labels are wrong. restorecon applies the file-context rule for /var/www, and httpd_t can read them again without widening the policy.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Privilege separation: OpenSSH's design case
question: Why does README.privsep insist that /var/empty is empty and not writable by the sshd user?
options: Because chroot only works on empty directories
So that a compromised child finds nothing to read and cannot plant files that a privileged process might later trust
So that log files go elsewhere
To save disk space
explain: The chroot is the child's whole view of the filesystem. Empty means nothing to steal; not writable means nothing to tamper with or leave for others.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Sandboxes: Chrome's broker model, macOS and iOS
question: Why does an iOS app's entitlements list need to be signed?
options: To make the app start faster
So that a compromised or modified app cannot grant itself new privileges by editing the list
Because Apple charges per entitlement
Entitlements are not signed
explain: Entitlements are signed with the app, so changing them breaks the signature. The platform can then trust the list when deciding what the app may do.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Kernel bugs and container escapes: Dirty Pipe and runc
question: Which setting, according to the runc maintainers, blocked CVE-2019-5736?
options: Docker's default seccomp profile
The default AppArmor profile
A read-only container root filesystem
Running containers in user namespaces where host root is not mapped into the container
explain: The advisory says the attack is not blocked by default AppArmor (nor by Fedora's moby-engine SELinux domain), but is blocked by correct use of user namespaces: container root is then an unprivileged host UID that cannot write /usr/bin/runc.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Requirements and collection plans: decide before you search
question: In the Berkeley Protocol's cycle, what is the preliminary assessment for?
options: Writing the final report
Publishing early results
Deciding whether found material is relevant and reliable enough to collect at all
Hashing collected files
explain: Preliminary assessment sits between inquiry and collection so that irrelevant or unreliable material is never collected. Hashing belongs to collection and preservation.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
question: A video downloaded from a social platform has a creation date one day after the event it claims to show. What is the best conclusion?
options: The metadata may describe the platform's re-encoded copy; corroborate the date by other means
The video is fake
The event happened a day later than reported
Metadata is always accurate, so the uploader lied
explain: The Berkeley Protocol notes that platforms transcode uploads, so metadata may reflect the new file, not the original. A date mismatch is a question to investigate, not a verdict.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Case: MH17 and the open-source trail of a missile launcher
question: What made the 17 July timeline in Bellingcat's report persuasive?
options: Several independent kinds of timing evidence (stated times, shadows, timestamped posts) agreed with one route
A single high-resolution photo
A confession posted online
The number of people who shared the photos
explain: Independent methods agreeing is what makes a timeline robust. Sharing counts are popularity, not evidence, and no single photo carried the case.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
question: Your report includes a finding that a public spreadsheet lists staff home addresses. How should the report present it?
options: Describe the exposure, location of the file and fix, without reproducing the addresses
Paste the spreadsheet into an appendix for completeness
Leave it out, since it is not about systems
List the addresses of senior staff only
explain: The finding is the exposure; reproducing personal data spreads it further. It is in scope because it enables social engineering against the organisation.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Parallel builds: jobs, RAM and the critical path
question: A 32-core, 32 GB workstation keeps failing a CUDA build with a compiler process "killed" at random files. Each nvcc job peaks near 4 GB. What should you try first?
options: Raise -j to 64 so the build finishes before memory fills
Switch the build type to Debug
Limit parallelism to about 32 / 4 = 8 jobs (for example -j 8 or MAX_JOBS=8)
Delete CMakeCache.txt
explain: Ninja's default would run 34 jobs, about 136 GB at peak. Capping at RAM divided by per-job peak keeps the build alive. More jobs make it worse, and the cache is unrelated.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
question: A parametrized test has node ids `test_pad[left]` and `test_pad[right]`. Only `right` fails in CI. Which command runs just that case?
options: `pytest tests/test_text.py::test_pad`
`pytest 'tests/test_text.py::test_pad[right]'`
`pytest -m right`
`pytest -k pad --lf`
explain: Parameters are part of the node id in square brackets; quote it so the shell does not treat the brackets as a glob. The bare function id runs both cases, `-m` selects by marker not parameter, and `--lf` depends on your local cache, which knows nothing about CI's failures.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
question: A reviewer asks you to also refactor an unrelated module your PR happens to call. The request is reasonable but would double the PR's size. What is the best move?
options: Do the refactor in this PR so the reviewer approves
Explain it is out of scope, open an issue to track it, and link the issue in your reply
Ignore the comment since it is not about your change
Close the PR and start over with both changes
explain: Ignoring a comment is the one thing every guide warns against. Folding unrelated work in makes the PR harder to review. GitHub's docs suggest opening an issue for out-of-scope feedback, which keeps the PR focused and the suggestion from getting lost.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
question: Which community health file can NOT be provided as an account-wide default from the `.github` repository?
options: CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
SECURITY.md
LICENSE
Issue templates
explain: GitHub's docs say you cannot create a default license file: it must live in each repository so it is included when the project is cloned, packaged or downloaded. Defaults in the `.github` repository are not part of clones.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
question: You open a PR from YOU/repo branch `fix-parser` into ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo `main`. Which is the base branch?
options: `fix-parser` in your fork
`main` in your fork
`main` in the upstream repository
`upstream/main` in your local clone
explain: The base branch is where the changes would be merged: the upstream repository's `main`. The compare (head) branch is `fix-parser` in your fork. `upstream/main` is only your local bookmark and does not exist on GitHub.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
question: Your 3-commit PR is merged with "Rebase and merge". Back in your clone, `git fetch upstream` then `git log upstream/main` does not show 7af2db7. Why?
options: GitHub dropped your commits because they were signed off
Rebase and merge recreates each commit with new SHAs and updated committer information
Your fetch is stale and needs to be repeated
Rebase and merge always squashes into one commit
explain: GitHub's docs say Rebase and merge always updates the committer information and creates new commit SHAs. Your changes are there, but as new commits with the same content and messages. Squashing is a different merge method.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
question: A one-line typo fix to an Apache project arrives from someone with no ICLA. Under what terms does the ASF receive it?
options: It cannot be accepted until an ICLA is signed
Under Apache-2.0 section 5, as small contributions are
Under no terms: the ASF must rewrite it
Under the contributor's employer's license
explain: The ASF states that small contributions are made under clause 5 of Apache-2.0; ICLAs are required for committers and for large contributions.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Reporting honestly: geomeans, many benchmarks and costs
question: A suite has 3 benchmarks with time ratios (new/old) 0.50, 2.00 and 1.00. What does the geometric mean say, and what would the arithmetic mean of ratios say?
options: Geomean 1.00 (no change); arithmetic mean 1.17 (17% slower)
Geomean 1.17; arithmetic mean 1.00
Both say 1.00
Geomean 0.50; arithmetic mean 2.00
explain: The product 0.5 x 2 x 1 = 1, so the geomean is 1.00: a halving and a doubling cancel. The arithmetic mean (0.5 + 2 + 1)/3 = 1.17 is pulled up by the slowdown, which is why suite summaries use the geometric mean of ratios.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Find the commit behind a change: log -S, -G and -L
question: A security check `if (!is_admin(user))` used to exist in auth.c and is gone today. Which command finds the commit that deleted it?
options: `git blame auth.c`
`git grep is_admin`
`git log -S'is_admin(user)' -- auth.c`
`git log --follow auth.c` and read every diff
explain: Deleting the check lowers the number of occurrences of that text, which is exactly what -S finds. blame and grep only see lines that exist now. Reading every diff works but is what the pickaxe automates.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
question: At some old commits the project fails to build because of an unrelated, since-fixed toolchain problem. What should your bisect script do at those commits?
options: Exit 125 so git skips them and tests a nearby commit instead
Exit 1, because a failing build is a failure
Exit 0, because the bug cannot be present if nothing was built
explain: 125 means "cannot test". Exit 1 would mark the commit bad and steer the search toward the build breakage instead of your bug; exit 0 would mark it good when you actually do not know. Both give a wrong answer.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
question: You want early feedback on whether your approach to a cache fix is acceptable, but tests are still failing. What is the best move?
options: Open a normal PR and ask code owners to ignore the failures
Wait until the change is finished before showing anyone
Open a normal PR with "WIP" in the title so it cannot be merged
Open a draft PR, state the open question in the description, and mark it ready once tests pass
explain: A draft cannot be merged and does not auto-request code owners, so it is the right tool for early feedback. A WIP title is only a convention: GitHub does not block merging on it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
question: Why does vLLM evict all of a sequence's blocks at once instead of picking the least recently used blocks like an OS?
options: Every decode step attends over all of the sequence's earlier tokens, so a partially evicted sequence cannot run anyway
GPU memory only supports freeing whole requests
LRU needs timestamps that GPUs cannot record
Partial eviction would break the block size invariant
explain: Attention reads every previous token's KV, so a sequence with any block missing cannot take its next step. The paper therefore evicts all or none of a sequence's blocks, and gang-schedules sequences that share blocks, such as beam candidates.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefix caching across a fleet and behind an API
question: A router uses an approximate prefix index (it assumes a prefix stays on the replica it was last sent to). Replicas are short on memory and evict often. What do you expect?
options: Hit rates match the router's predictions, because eviction is rare in practice
Outputs become wrong when the router's guess is stale
The router keeps choosing replicas that already evicted the prefix, so predicted hits turn into full prefills and load piles up on those replicas; KV events from the engines would correct the index
Requests fail with an out-of-memory error at the router
explain: The approximate index tracks routing decisions, not engine state. Under memory pressure the two drift apart: requests are steered toward a replica for a cache it no longer has, paying both the prefill and the locality-driven imbalance. Results stay correct, since a miss just recomputes; only speed suffers.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Methodologies: PTES, NIST SP 800-115 and the OWASP guide
question: Why does NIST describe reporting as running alongside the other phases rather than only at the end?
options: Because logs and status updates during the test let the client match activity to the test and react to critical issues early
Because reports are written by a separate team
Because reporting is optional
Because the client pays per page
explain: Logs and periodic reports during discovery and attack are part of the method: they protect both sides and let urgent findings be fixed before the final report.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reading Nmap output: ports, services, versions and guesses
question: Why should an Nmap OS guess such as 'Linux 2.6.39' be reported with care?
options: It is always exact
Nmap never guesses operating systems
OS detection reads the version from the login banner
It is inferred from how the TCP/IP stack behaves, which firewalls, load balancers and unusual stacks can distort
explain: OS detection matches packet behaviour against a fingerprint database. A middlebox answering on the host's behalf changes the fingerprint, so treat the result as an inference.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
question: While verifying a finding you notice a file named `human2.aspx` in a MOVEit web root, next to the legitimate `human.aspx`. What do you do?
options: Stop testing that system and call the emergency contact: it matches a published indicator of a real compromise
Open the file to see how it works
Delete it to help the client
Note it in the final report and carry on
explain: CISA's advisory names human2.aspx as the LEMURLOOT web shell masquerading as human.aspx. Touching or deleting it destroys evidence; the right move is to halt and hand over to incident response.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
question: A teammate says: 'The profile shows parse_header in 0.4% of 990 samples, so it costs 0.4% of runtime, and the call count must be small.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing, both conclusions follow from the profile
Sampling overcounts short functions, so the real share is lower
0.4% of 990 is about 4 samples, so the share is very uncertain, and sampling says nothing about call counts
perf only samples the main thread, so the share is wrong
explain: Four samples give a very rough estimate (the margin is about as large as the value), and a sampler never sees calls, only which code was on the CPU when the timer fired. A function could be called a million times and still appear rarely if each call is tiny.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
question: After a fix, convolve drops from 40% to 30% of the flame graph. Which statement is safest?
options: The program is now 10% faster
convolve now takes a smaller share of on-CPU samples; measure total runtime or CPU time to know if the program got faster
convolve is now called 25% less often
Other functions got slower
explain: Widths are shares of each profile's own total. A share can drop because convolve got faster or because something else grew. Pair the flame graph with an absolute measurement (runtime, CPU seconds, sample counts at a fixed rate and duration).

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
question: A transaction updates 12 small, scattered fields and is on a hot path. Under the course's simple fence model, which logging style and why?
options: Undo: it needs 3 fences regardless of size
Redo: about 3 fences instead of 14, at the cost of reads inside the transaction checking the log
Neither: 12 fields is small enough to update with 12 independent 8-byte stores safely
Undo: its reads go to the log, which is faster
explain: With k = 12, undo costs k + 2 = 14 fences in the model and redo costs 3. Twelve independent 8-byte stores are each atomic but not atomic together, so the transaction could tear. Undo reads go to data in place; redo is the one with log lookups.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: How an email actually moves: SMTP and MX records
question: A message has three Received headers. Which one was written by your own receiving server, and what in it can you trust most?
options: The top one; the IP address your server saw on the TCP connection
The bottom one; the EHLO name
The middle one; the date
Any of them; all Received headers are verified by DNS
explain: Servers prepend, so your server's header is on top. Its IP address came from the actual connection, while the EHLO name is whatever the client chose to say. Lower headers could have been written by anyone, including the sender.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DKIM: a signature over headers and body
question: A mailing list adds '[team]' to every Subject. The original signature listed Subject in h=. What happens to the original DKIM signature?
options: Nothing, Subject is never signed
It still verifies because relaxed canonicalization ignores added words
It fails, because a signed header changed
It is automatically re-signed by the original domain
explain: Relaxed canonicalization tolerates whitespace and header-name case, not new words. A changed signed header means the signature no longer verifies.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Malicious links, attachments and HTML smuggling
question: A gateway inspects every attachment's file type and blocks executables. Why does HTML smuggling get past it?
options: The executable is created by JavaScript in the recipient's browser, so it never crosses the gateway as a file
The gateway cannot read HTML
HTML attachments are encrypted by SMTP
Executables inside HTML are always signed
explain: The gateway sees only an HTML document. The payload exists as encoded data and becomes a file only on the endpoint, which is why endpoint and browser controls matter here.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
question: Lain et al. found one human-centred measure clearly effective at company scale. Which?
options: Embedded training pages after a simulated click
Monthly mandatory quizzes
Punishing repeat clickers
Employees collectively reporting suspicious emails via a report button
explain: Crowd-sourced reporting detected new campaigns fast with acceptable operational load, and employees stayed active over long periods. Embedded training did not help and could backfire.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
question: Which change can never shrink a C struct?
options: Moving the char fields to the end
Reordering fields so larger alignments come first
Moving a pointer field from the end to the front of a struct whose other fields are all pointers
Replacing an int field with a short when the values fit
explain: If every field is a pointer, every offset is already a multiple of 8 and there is no padding to remove, so moving one pointer changes nothing. The other options can each remove padding or bytes.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Layout for the cache: arrays of structs versus structs of arrays
question: Eight threads each update `counts[t]` in `long counts[8];`, and it runs slower with 8 threads than with 1. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: The array is misaligned; use aligned_alloc(8, ...)
long is too small; use int64_t
All eight counters share one 64-byte line; give each its own line with alignas(64) or padding
The compiler reorders the array; mark it volatile
explain: 8 x 8 = 64 bytes, so the counters fit in one 64-byte line, or two if the array straddles a boundary, and every write steals a line from the other cores: false sharing. Padding each counter to its own line removes the traffic, as the measurement in this lesson showed.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
question: A drone films a stadium crowd of 200 people from far away, and you need rough poses on a fixed compute budget. Which design fits better?
options: Top-down, because it is more accurate on COCO
Top-down with a larger crop size
Either; the cost is identical
Bottom-up, because one network pass covers everyone and cost barely grows with 200 people
explain: Top-down would run the keypoint network 200 times per frame. Bottom-up runs once and groups with cheap matching. Accuracy per person may be lower, but the cost model favors bottom-up at this crowd size.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Shor's algorithm in outline: factoring is period finding
question: X25519 key exchange involves no factoring at all. Why does Shor's algorithm still break it?
options: It doesn't: only RSA is affected
Shor's paper also solves discrete logarithms with the same period-finding idea, and X25519 rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm
X25519 secretly uses RSA for authentication
Grover's algorithm breaks 128-bit curves
explain: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for both factoring and discrete logarithms. Recovering an X25519 private scalar from a recorded public key is a discrete-log problem, which is exactly what harvest-now-decrypt-later relies on.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Inside ML-KEM: modules, compression and the FO transform
question: A developer wants to use K-PKE directly to encrypt 32-byte messages because it is simpler than the KEM. What does FIPS 203 say?
options: It is approved for short messages
K-PKE shall not be used as a stand-alone scheme; it is only a component of ML-KEM
It is allowed only with ML-KEM-1024
It is approved if the messages are random
explain: FIPS 203 Section 3.3 states that K-PKE is not approved as a public-key encryption scheme. It is not IND-CCA2 secure; the KEM is.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Hybrid designs: combiners, Signal, iMessage and SSH
question: You design a file-encryption format that combines X25519 and ML-KEM-768. Which key derivation is the safest choice?
options: K = K1 XOR K2
K = SHA-256(K1 || K2), because concatenation is what TLS does
K = SHA3-256(K1 || K2 || c1 || c2 || ek1 || ek2 || label naming the format and version)
K = K1 alone, with K2 sent as a backup
explain: TLS 1.3's concatenation is safe because of its transcript hashing. A standalone format has no transcript, and SP 800-227 shows KDF(K1, K2) alone does not generically preserve IND-CCA security; binding ciphertexts, keys and a domain label does.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
question: A pgvector query uses HNSW with ef_search = 40, WHERE tenant_id = 7 (0.5% of rows) and LIMIT 10. It usually returns 0 rows. What is the cause?
options: The HNSW graph is corrupted and needs a REINDEX
The filter runs after a 40-candidate scan; with s = 0.005 the expected survivors are 0.2, and P(zero) = 0.995^40 is about 82%
LIMIT 10 is applied before the WHERE clause, so the planner discards matches
HNSW cannot index tables that contain a tenant_id column
explain: Post-filtering on 40 candidates gives 40 x 0.005 = 0.2 expected matches, and the probability of none is 0.995^40 = 0.82. The index is fine; the filter just sees too few candidates. Iterative scans, a partial index, or a B-tree driven exact scan fix it (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Estimating selectivity, and correlated filters
question: A planner using lesson 4's cost model (n = 10 million, k = 10, c = 10) estimates 50,000 matches, but only 800 vectors truly match. Which plan runs, and what does it cost?
options: Brute force, 800 distances, since the plan is always fixed after execution starts
Brute force, 50,000 distances, because the planner trusts the estimate
The graph walk, about 20,000 distances, exactly as estimated
The graph walk: chosen because 20,000 beats 50,000 at the estimated s, but at the true s = 0.00008 it costs about 1,250,000 instead of the 800 brute force needs
explain: At the estimate s = 0.005 the model gives brute force 50,000 and graph 10 x 10 / 0.005 = 20,000, so it picks the graph. The walk's real cost follows the true s: 100 / 0.00008 = 1,250,000. Brute force on the true count would have cost 800.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
question: A core keeps 16 lines in flight and memory latency rises from 80 ns to 120 ns. Peak DRAM bandwidth is not the limit. What happens to this core's bandwidth?
options: It stays at 12.8 GB/s because peak bandwidth did not change
It drops to about 8.5 GB/s
It rises, because longer latency means more lines are in flight
It drops to 0.8 GB/s
explain: With concurrency capped at 16 lines, $B = 16 \times 64 / 120 \approx 8.53$ GB/s. Little's law says bandwidth is concurrency divided by latency, so longer latency at fixed concurrency means less bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
question: A fitness app encrypts all routes, has no breaches, and starts using routes to set prices for a partner insurer without telling users. Which NIST privacy engineering objective is most directly violated?
options: Confidentiality, because the data left the app
Predictability, because users cannot reliably anticipate this use of their data
Availability, because users lose control of their routes
Integrity, because the routes were changed
explain: Nothing was disclosed to an unauthorised party and nothing was altered or made unavailable. The problem is a use people could not anticipate: predictability. Confidentiality is a security objective about unauthorised access, and the insurer use here is authorised by the operator.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Location traces and aggregate maps: Strava 2018
question: de Montjoye and colleagues found that four hourly, antenna-level points identify 95 percent of people. What does coarsening the location resolution do?
options: Makes traces anonymous after one step
Reduces uniqueness only slowly, roughly as the 1/10 power of the resolution
Increases uniqueness
Has no effect
explain: The paper reports uniqueness decaying approximately as the 1/10 power of resolution: coarser data helps, but not enough on its own. That is why location needs stronger tools than rounding.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
question: An analyst asks for the same noisy count 100 times, each at epsilon = 0.1, and averages the answers. What is the privacy cost?
options: 0.1, because it is the same question
10, because composition adds the epsilons
0.001, because averaging reduces noise
Zero, because the answers are noisy
explain: Each independent noisy answer spends 0.1; 100 of them spend 10. Averaging improves accuracy exactly because it removes the protection. Serve repeats from a cache instead.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
question: Why is non-repudiation a threat in LINDDUN when it is a security goal in STRIDE?
options: LINDDUN disagrees with STRIDE about logging
Because for users, undeniable evidence of what they did or said can harm them, for example read receipts or signed records of a vote
Because non-repudiation requires encryption
Because GDPR forbids audit logs
explain: Evidence that protects a system (an admin audit log) can harm an individual where deniability matters. The designer decides per flow which property applies.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
question: An attacker emails support from a lookalike address asking for 'all data you hold about me' for a victim's account. What control matters most?
options: Encrypting the export
Verifying the requester's identity in proportion to the data, for example by requiring the request from the authenticated account
Replying within one month
Deleting the data instead
explain: The risk is disclosure to an impostor. Proportionate identity verification (the ICO allows asking for information needed to confirm identity) and delivery to a verified channel prevent it; encryption does not help if you send it to the attacker.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 3: setuid, capabilities, kernel bugs, docker group
question: A contractor's account is in the docker group but has no sudo rights. How should an access review classify it?
options: Unprivileged: no sudo means no root
Root-equivalent: the docker group can start containers that write the host filesystem as root
Low risk unless the account also has a password
Privileged only inside containers
explain: Docker's own documentation says the docker group grants root-level privileges, because the root daemon will mount the host filesystem into a container on request. Review it exactly like a sudo ALL rule.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
question: An intruder has code running as an ordinary user on a laptop, with no admin rights yet. Which store can they most likely read immediately?
options: LSASS memory
The SAM hive
The user's browser password store
Other users' SSH keys
explain: Browser stores have traditionally been decrypted with the user's own logon credentials, so code running as that user can read them (Chrome's newer App-Bound Encryption, starting with cookies, raises that bar). LSASS and SAM need admin or SYSTEM, and other users' home directories are normally not readable.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Pivoting and tunnelling: reaching networks you cannot reach
question: Why does protocol tunnelling not make the activity invisible to network defenders?
options: Tunnels are always unencrypted
The outer connection still shows its endpoints, timing, duration and volume
Firewalls decrypt all SSH traffic by default
Tunnels only work over UDP
explain: Encapsulation hides the inner protocol, not the outer flow. A web server holding a long SSH session to an unusual host, or moving steady traffic for hours, stands out in flow and firewall logs without any decryption.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: You double the number of rollouts per step from 8 to 16 to 'make the labels more accurate', using hard estimation. Which error grows?
options: Correct steps labeled bad, because more rollouts mean more failures
Wrong steps labeled good, because more rollouts give a lucky recovery more chances to occur
Neither; HE labels converge to the truth as N grows
Both shrink equally
explain: HE marks a step good if any rollout succeeds. P(at least one recovery) = 1 - (1-r)^N rises with N, so wrong steps get marked good more often. Correct-step false negatives (1-q)^N fall. Math-Shepherd observed exactly this: larger N led to false positives.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
question: Which of these was NOT one of DeepSeek-R1's stated reasons for not using a PRM in large-scale RL?
options: Defining a fine-grained step in general reasoning is hard
Judging intermediate-step correctness is hard, and manual labels do not scale
A model-based PRM leads to reward hacking and retraining adds overhead
PRMs cannot rerank top-N responses or assist guided search
explain: DeepSeek-R1 says the opposite: PRMs show good ability to rerank top-N responses and assist guided search. Their objection was that the benefit in large-scale RL did not outweigh the extra compute and complexity.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: A process's life: exec, exit, wait, zombies and orphans
question: A service holds a database connection on file descriptor 7, then runs an untrusted helper with `fork()` plus `execve()`. Which statement is true?
options: The helper inherits fd 7, still open, unless it was marked close-on-exec, so the helper can use the connection
execve() closes every descriptor except 0, 1 and 2
fd 7 is open in the helper but refers to a fresh copy of the socket
The helper cannot see fd 7 because execve() gives it a new PID
explain: execve() keeps the PID and keeps descriptors open by default; only those marked FD_CLOEXEC are closed. Mark sensitive descriptors close-on-exec when you open them, or close them in the child before exec.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: A CPU-bound image service runs 64 worker threads on an 8-core machine. `nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches` climbs by thousands per second per thread, and p99 latency (the time that 99 percent of requests finish within) is high even though CPU is at 100 percent. What is the best first change?
options: Add more worker threads so each request is more likely to find one free
Cut the pool to about 8 workers and queue requests, so each runs to completion on a core
Raise the time slice so involuntary switches become voluntary
Move the workers into separate processes for isolation
explain: There are 8 times more runnable threads than cores, so threads keep preempting each other: high involuntary counts and late completions, as in the timeline. A core-sized pool with a queue removes most switches. Processes would make each switch more expensive, not rarer.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
question: An IVFPQ index with nlist = 1024 and PQ64 has poor recall. Profiling shows the true nearest neighbor is usually in the 3rd or 4th nearest list. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to PQ128 codes
Reduce nlist to 64 so lists are bigger
Turn off residual encoding
Increase nprobe from 1 to 8
explain: Neighbors in unprobed lists are never scored, so better codes cannot find them. Raising nprobe scans those lists. Shrinking nlist also captures them but scans a much larger fraction per probe; the paper finds that for a fixed fraction visited, more lists with more probes is more accurate.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Sizing and tuning an IVFPQ index for a memory budget
question: On SIFT1M, IVF4096,PQ32x4fsr,RFlat gives 42.3 percent recall@10 at nprobe 64 with k_factor 1. You need about 90. Which change does our sweep say to try first?
options: Raise nprobe to 256
Retrain with more lists
Switch to 8-bit PQ32
Raise k_factor to 10, so 100 candidates are re-ranked exactly
explain: At nprobe 64 the lists already contain most true neighbors; the 4-bit codes just rank them poorly. k_factor 10 moved recall to 89.4 at about the same time per query, while nprobe 256 with k_factor 1 reached only 42.4.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
question: You run DSPy's BootstrapRS without passing a valset. It reports 0.92 on 50 training examples, and 0.81 on your test set. What most likely explains the gap?
options: The valset defaulted to the trainset, so demos were bootstrapped from and selected on the same examples
BootstrapRS always reports accuracy times 1.1
The test set must be mislabelled
Random search cannot overfit
explain: Per the DSPy docs the valset defaults to the trainset. The selected program contains demos drawn from those same examples and was chosen for scoring well on them, so its training score is optimistic. Pass a separate valset and keep a test set apart.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: Why does the rotation part of the forward process use IGSO(3) instead of adding Gaussian noise to the nine entries of R?
options: IGSO(3) is faster to sample than a Gaussian
Because a Gaussian perturbation of the nine entries leaves a matrix that is not orthonormal, so it is not a rotation at all
Because rotations have nine degrees of freedom and Gaussians only model three
Because the loss must be invariant to global rotation
explain: SO(3) is a curved manifold embedded in 9-dimensional space. Adding independent Gaussian noise to the entries leaves the manifold: columns stop being orthonormal and the determinant stops being 1. IGSO(3) is the transition density of Brownian motion that stays on the manifold.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Lists, dictionaries and sets: counting what matters
question: You want to know whether an address appears in a list of 2 million known-bad addresses, checked once per log line. Which container should hold the bad addresses?
options: A list, because it keeps the order from the threat feed
A set, because membership checks do not slow down as it grows
A string with all addresses joined by commas
A list sorted alphabetically
explain: `x in some_list` compares against items one by one, so it gets slower as the list grows. A set (like dict keys) uses hashing to jump straight to the right slot. A joined string can also give false matches: `1.2.3.4` is inside `11.2.3.45`.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
question: Your detection searches web logs for a known-bad string and has never fired, but a colleague finds the string percent-encoded twice in last week's logs. What is the best fix?
options: Add the twice-encoded form as a second exact string
Decode each field repeatedly until it stops changing, then search the decoded text
Search only for the % character
Base64-encode the logs first
explain: Adding encoded variants one by one never ends: once, twice, mixed case hex, partial encoding. Normalizing the input to a fixed point and matching once covers all of them, with a round limit so hostile input cannot make you loop forever.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Testing your script so it does not fail silently
question: Why does test_enrich.py pass a FakeSession to lookup_hash instead of letting it call VirusTotal?
options: The real API does not support MD5
Tests should be fast, repeatable and offline: no quota, no key, and no failures caused by the network or by the service's data changing
pytest cannot import requests
Fakes make the code run in production too
explain: A test that depends on a live service fails for reasons unrelated to your code and spends real quota. Designing functions to receive their dependencies (here, the session) is what makes fakes possible.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
question: Why does Rocchio usually set gamma much smaller than beta?
options: Nonrelevant documents are rare, so their centroid is unstable
Manning et al. report positive feedback is much more valuable than negative feedback
A large gamma makes the query vector longer, which BM25 penalizes
gamma must equal 1 - beta for the vector to stay normalized
explain: Relevant documents tend to resemble each other; nonrelevant ones are scattered across many topics, so subtracting their centroid says little. Some systems allow only positive feedback, which is gamma = 0.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
question: A user searches `flew form Heathrow`. Your spelling corrector checks each word against a dictionary. What happens?
options: It rewrites form to from, because form is 2 edits from from
Nothing changes, because every word is a correctly spelled dictionary word
It rewrites Heathrow, because proper nouns are not in the dictionary
It asks did you mean, because the query returns zero results
explain: An isolated-term corrector only fires on words that are not in the dictionary. form is a real word, so it is left alone. Catching it needs context-sensitive correction, which scores combinations such as flew from by how often they occur together.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
question: A support bot gets "Which plan did I upgrade to after the billing change last March?" and the knowledge base has a general article on plan history. Which pattern fits best?
options: Step-Back: also retrieve for a broader question such as the account's plan change history
Multi-query with 3 paraphrases of the same narrow question
Spelling correction
Least-to-most on SCAN
explain: The question is narrow and time-specific, while the evidence lives in a general history document. Step-Back adds a broad query that retrieves it, and the reader picks the March change from it. Paraphrases of the narrow question share its narrowness.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
question: After rotation, the inner product between a data vector and its quantized vector is about 0.8 in high dimensions. What does this number mean?
options: The code is wrong in 20% of the bits
The estimator is accurate to within 0.2
The quantized vector is a unit vector at roughly 37 degrees from the data vector, so using it directly would shrink inner products
Only 80% of vectors get a valid code
explain: Both are unit vectors and their cosine is about 0.8 (about 37 degrees). Lesson 4 shows why treating o-bar as if it were o is biased, and how dividing by this stored 0.8-ish value fixes it.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Extended RaBitQ: finding the best multi-bit code
question: Why does the extended RaBitQ encoder only need to try finitely many rescaling factors t?
options: Because t must be an integer
Because the paper fixes t = 2^B for every vector
Because only the largest coordinate of o' depends on t
Because the rounded vector, and so its cosine with o', changes only when some t |o'_i| crosses a rounding boundary, at t = k / |o'_i|
explain: Rounding is piecewise constant: between two critical values no coordinate changes its rounded value, so the code and its cosine stay fixed. Checking each critical value once, in sorted order, covers every code that rounding t o' can produce, and Lemma 3.1 says the best code is among them.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Prices, quantities and negative numbers: validating what input means
question: A developer adds `min="1"` to the HTML quantity input and says the negative-quantity bug is fixed. What is the right response?
options: Agreed, browsers enforce min on every request
Not fixed: the field should be a dropdown instead
Agreed, as long as the form also uses HTTPS
Not fixed: the browser check helps honest users, but the server must reject quantities outside 1 to stock itself
explain: HTML attributes only shape what the browser offers. A request edited in a proxy, or sent with curl, never meets that check. Only a server-side range check enforces the rule.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Limit overrun: one coupon, one balance, many parallel requests
question: Why did the claim-first Node version give the right result with five parallel requests?
options: Because Promise.all runs promises one at a time
Because the check and the claim run with no await between them, so no other request's code can run in between, in this single process
Because Sets are thread-safe in every language
Because the fake database became faster
explain: Node only switches to other requests' code at an await. Putting the check and the claim in one synchronous step makes them atomic inside one process. That guarantee disappears as soon as the state lives in a database shared by several processes.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Idempotency keys: safe retries, and what they do not stop
question: Why does the idempotency layer reply 422 when a known key arrives with a different request body?
options: To hide whether the key exists
Because reusing a key for a different request is a client bug or misuse, and replaying the old response would answer a question that was not asked
Because 422 means the request was too large
Because HTTP forbids reusing headers
explain: The key promises "this is the same operation as before". If the body differs, either the client generated keys wrongly or someone is probing. Replaying the stored result would silently ignore the new request; the draft and Stripe both reject it instead.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
question: A 5-server cluster is split by a network failure into a group of 2 servers and a group of 3. Which side can still commit new commands?
options: Both sides, and they reconcile later
Only the side with 3 servers
Only the side that holds the current leader
Neither side until the network heals
explain: Committing needs a majority of the full cluster, which is 3 of 5. Only the 3-server side has one. If the old leader is on the 2-server side, it can keep accepting requests but can never commit them; the 3-server side elects a new leader and keeps going.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft safety: the election restriction and the Figure 8 trap
question: A new leader is elected in term 6. Its log ends with entries from term 5 that are on a majority but not known to be committed, and no client requests arrive. What lets it learn which of those entries are committed?
options: Nothing: it must wait for the next client write
Counting replicas of the term-5 entries, since they are on a majority
Asking followers for their commitIndex and taking the maximum
Appending and committing a no-op entry in term 6
explain: Older-term entries cannot be committed by counting replicas. The paper has each new leader commit a blank no-op entry at the start of its term; once that term-6 entry commits, every entry before it is committed too. This matters for reads, as lesson 6 shows.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
question: With the toy budget of 60 words, a teammate proposes Strategy A with k = 3 because D1 ranks first and contains both facts. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; 3 whole documents fit in 60 words
D1 is dropped because whole documents cannot be ranked
The three documents total 93 words, so D6 and D2 do not fit; fill-in-rank-order keeps D1 alone, which happens to be enough here but leaves no room for a second source
The answer reserve grows automatically to fit
explain: D1 (44) + D6 (24) + D2 (25) = 93 words, over the 60-word context budget. Whole-document chunks spend the budget fast; here D1 alone holds both facts, but for any question needing two documents this strategy fails.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
question: A food-delivery search ranks restaurants. Which of these is a query-document feature?
options: The restaurant's average rating
The number of words the user typed
BM25 of the query against the restaurant's menu text
The hour of the day the restaurant opened
explain: Menu BM25 needs both the query and the restaurant, so it is query-document. Rating and opening hour describe only the restaurant (document features), and word count describes only the query (a query feature).

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
question: Which normalization lets the model compare match strength across queries, so it can tell that the best json match is weak?
options: A global transform with fixed constants, such as min-max fitted on the whole training set
Per-query min-max (LETOR QueryLevelNorm)
Both preserve it equally
Neither, BM25 cannot be compared across documents
explain: A global transform applies the same constants to every query, so a raw 0.43 stays lower than a raw 1.08. Per-query min-max maps every query's best document to 1, erasing that difference.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
question: Your product shows one answer card for factual questions, and a second correct answer has no extra value. Which metric fits best?
options: Recall@10
Linear-gain nDCG@10
ERR or reciprocal rank
MAP
explain: The user is satisfied by the first good result, which is the cascade assumption. RR handles binary labels; ERR adds graded labels. Recall, MAP and nDCG all reward finding more relevant documents, which this product does not value.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Trust among thieves: exit scams, takedowns and a fragmented market
question: Coveware reports that by Q3 2026 no group held more than 6% of its cases. What is the best practical response for a detection team?
options: Write rules for the top six group names each quarter
Focus detections on techniques that recur across groups, such as remote access tools, AD enumeration and bulk exfiltration
Stop monitoring for ransomware, since the market is collapsing
Rely on file hashes of each new encryptor
explain: Affiliates move between brands and many work alone, so names and hashes churn faster than rules can follow. Techniques recur because the job (get in, get admin, steal, encrypt) does not change. The market fragmenting does not mean attacks stopped.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
question: Witty testified the company cut connectivity to its data centres before knowing how the attackers got in. What is the main justification?
options: Without knowing the entry point or spread, isolating everything was the surest way to stop the malware reaching other parts of the health system
It preserved evidence on the encrypted servers
It forced the attackers to lower the ransom
It is required by HIPAA (the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)
explain: Witty said the cut was made to eliminate the potential for further infection, and that no spread beyond Change was found. Broad isolation costs availability but buys certainty when scope is unknown, the same reasoning Colonial Pipeline used. It is not mainly about evidence or price.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Backups that survive an attacker with Domain Admin
question: Your backups go to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in governance mode. The backup server's IAM role has s3:BypassGovernanceRetention. An attacker owns the backup server. Are the backups safe?
options: No: with that permission the role can override governance retention and delete the objects
Yes: Object Lock always prevents deletion
Yes, because only the root user can delete objects
No, because Object Lock does not work with backups
explain: AWS documents that governance mode can be overridden by principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention sending the bypass header. The fix is compliance mode, or at least removing that permission from anything production can reach, ideally in a separate account.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue
question: This code posts a signaled SEND of `buf`, then immediately does `memcpy(buf, next_msg, 64)` and posts another SEND of `buf`, and only then polls the CQ. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: ibv_post_send copies the payload before it returns
The first message may go out containing bytes of next_msg, because the NIC may still be reading buf
The second post fails because only one WR may be outstanding
The CQ will overflow after two posts
explain: Posting only queues a WQE that points at buf; the NIC reads the payload later by DMA. Overwriting buf before the first completion is a race. Either wait for the completion, use a second buffer, or (for small payloads) set IBV_SEND_INLINE so the data is copied into the WQE at post time.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
question: Why did the fetch-and-add sequencer lose to an RPC design even though it never touches the server CPU?
options: Atomics are not supported on RC
All requests serialize on a lock inside the NIC, held for a PCIe round trip each
Atomics use UD and drop packets
The CPU is interrupted for each atomic
explain: Kalia et al. explain that NIC processing units take an internal lock for the target address and do a read-modify-write over PCIe, holding it for hundreds of nanoseconds. One hot counter turns into a serial queue.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
question: You raise the tick rate from 10 to 50 per second. One-way latency is 80 ms. Roughly how much does a dumb client's average own-input delay drop?
options: From about 210 ms to about 170 ms
From about 160 ms to about 32 ms
It does not change; only bandwidth changes
From about 210 ms to about 42 ms
explain: Mean delay is 2d + T/2. At T = 100 ms: 160 + 50 = 210 ms. At T = 20 ms: 160 + 10 = 170 ms. The round trip of 160 ms is untouched by tick rate, which is why prediction is needed.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
question: Amazon's item-to-item design is described as fast even for huge catalogs. What makes the online request cheap?
options: Its cost depends on how many items this user has bought or rated, because neighbours are looked up in a precomputed table
It compares the user with every other customer, but uses cosine, which is cheap
It clusters customers into segments and only scores the user's segment
It recomputes item similarities for each request using only popular items
explain: Linden et al. build the similar-items table offline (worst case O(N^2 M) for N catalog items and M customers, closer to O(NM) in practice). The online step aggregates neighbours of the user's own items, so it scales independently of catalog size and customer count.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
question: A new item has rich metadata but zero interactions. Which model can rank it on day one?
options: Matrix factorization with an ID embedding table, retrained nightly
Item-to-item CF using co-purchase cosine
A two-tower model whose item tower reads content features
LinUCB with the item's ID as the only feature
explain: ID-based matrix factorization and co-purchase similarity both need interactions involving the item. An item tower over content features produces a vector from metadata alone, which can be indexed and retrieved immediately.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: ArUco markers, camera calibration and solvePnP
question: After calibrating a phone camera, the app lets the camera autofocus between shots. Why might measurements drift?
options: Autofocus changes the ArUco dictionary
Autofocus re-orders the detected corners
Refocusing has no effect on geometry, so they should not drift
Refocusing changes the optics, so the calibrated intrinsics and distortion may no longer match
explain: The OpenCV ArUco tutorial says calibration is valid unless the camera optics are modified, giving a change of focus as the example. A homography-only pipeline is less affected because it refits H from the marker in every photo, but undistortion still uses the stored coefficients.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
question: A plan estimates `rows=1` for a nested loop's outer input, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 200,000 actual rows and the query is slow. What is the best first fix?
options: Set enable_nestloop = off for the whole server
Raise work_mem so the nested loop fits in memory
Fix the estimate: run ANALYZE, add extended statistics for correlated columns, or add an index
Raise geqo_threshold so more join orders are searched
explain: The nested loop was chosen because of the 1-row estimate; the algorithm is a symptom. Correcting statistics lets the planner cost the alternatives honestly. Disabling nested loops globally hurts the many queries where an index nested loop is best, and work_mem and GEQO do not affect this estimate.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
question: A Cassandra replica was down for 5 hours with default settings, then rejoins. Some writes it missed were never read since. What brings it up to date?
options: Hint replay, since hints are kept until delivered
Nothing ever; the data is lost on that replica forever
Gossip automatically copies all missed rows on rejoin
Anti-entropy repair, because hints stop being generated after the 3 hour window and no reads triggered read repair
explain: Hints are generated only for the first `max_hint_window` (3 hours by default) of downtime. Writes after that are not hinted, and read repair only fixes keys that get read. A Merkle-tree repair (`nodetool repair`) is what restores those keys.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Goodhart measured: gold reward rises, then falls
question: In Gao et al., a 6B policy and a 1.2B policy are optimized against the same proxy RM. What did they observe about overoptimization?
options: Both peaked at almost the same KL, with a similar proxy-to-gold gap
The 6B policy overoptimized much faster because it is a stronger optimizer
The 6B policy never overoptimized
Only the 1.2B policy reached a peak
explain: Contrary to the intuition that bigger policies exploit RMs faster, gold scores peaked at almost the same KL and the proxy-gold gap was nearly the same. The larger policy did start higher and gained less from optimization.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
question: You run GRPO on coding tasks with reward = 1 if pytest exits successfully. Which change most directly closes the hacks in this lesson?
options: Lower the learning rate so hacks are learned more slowly
Run the grader outside the agent's sandbox on fresh copies of the tests, check results per test instead of the exit status, and remove reference solutions from the environment
Increase the group size from 4 to 16
Add a format reward for well-commented code
explain: Each hack exploits something the agent can touch: the exit status, the test files, pytest internals, or leftover answers. Isolating the grader removes those levers. A lower learning rate or bigger group changes how fast or how noisily the hack spreads, not whether it pays.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
question: Risk R-002 was accepted by the CTO until 30 June 2026. It is now November 2026 and nothing changed. What is the correct status?
options: Accepted, because the risk score did not change
Closed, because no incident happened
Transferred to the CTO personally
Unmanaged until someone with authority re-accepts it or treats it, because the acceptance has expired
explain: Acceptances expire on purpose so that someone re-examines the risk as the world changes. An expired acceptance means nobody currently owns the decision, which is exactly what reviewers look for.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Security economics: how much to spend (the Gordon-Loeb model)
question: Which statement is the model's main limitation in practice?
options: It cannot handle money
It needs the breach-probability function S(z, v), which nobody knows precisely for a real organisation
It says security spending is never worth it
It only applies to class III functions
explain: The shape of S is an assumption. The model is a way of thinking about diminishing returns and caps, not a calculator you can feed a real budget into.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
question: Requirement 3.3.1 says sensitive authentication data must not be stored after authorisation. A developer proposes keeping CVV codes encrypted with a strong key 'for retries'. Allowed?
options: Yes, if encrypted with AES-256
No: SAD must not be stored after authorisation even if encrypted
Yes, for up to 30 days
Only for SAQ merchants
explain: The requirement explicitly says 'even if encrypted'. Retry flows must use the provider's tokens or stored-credential mechanisms instead.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
question: Which part of the SEC's SolarWinds case survived the July 2024 motion to dismiss?
options: The internal accounting controls claim
Fraud claims based on the public Security Statement's access control and password claims
Claims based on post-attack press releases
Nothing; the whole case was dismissed in 2024
explain: Judge Engelmayer sustained the Security Statement fraud claims and dismissed the rest. The remaining case was dismissed by stipulation in November 2025.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
question: The OCC's 2020 penalty against Capital One focused mainly on which failure?
options: Using a cloud provider at all
Governance: no effective risk assessment before the cloud migration, internal audit not reporting weaknesses to the audit committee, and a board that did not hold management accountable
Not having a bug bounty programme
Paying the attacker
explain: The consent order's findings were about risk assessment, internal audit and board oversight, the governance roles from lesson 1.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Colocated or disaggregated: where the engines live
question: A team runs disaggregated pools with strict on-policy synchronous training and sees each pool idle about half the time. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Switch to FP8 weights for the rollout engine
Increase the KV cache size
Either colocate the pools or let rollout of the next batch overlap training on the current one with bounded staleness
Add more training GPUs
explain: Strict alternation between two separate pools means each pool waits for the other. Colocation lets one pool do both phases; overlap keeps both pools busy at the cost of one or more steps of staleness. The other changes speed up one phase but keep the alternation.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: Your synchronous colocated run spends 80% of each step in rollout, and one response in each batch runs to the 32k cap. Which plan addresses the root cause with the least algorithmic risk first?
options: Fully async with staleness 16 and no importance correction
Add training GPUs
Partial rollouts or a one-step overlap with bounded staleness and decoupled importance weights, then measure accuracy against a synchronous baseline
Lower the cap to 2k tokens
explain: The root cause is waiting on the long tail. Partial rollouts or a small, bounded staleness keep GPUs busy while keeping data nearly on-policy, and the decoupled objective corrects what remains. Large unbounded staleness risks learning quality; more trainers do not touch rollout; a tight cap truncates real reasoning.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
question: A vendor releases a GPU with twice the Tensor Core FLOP/s of its predecessor and the same memory bandwidth. Which kernel speeds up the most?
options: A batch 1 GEMV at 1 FLOP/byte
A large square GEMM at about 1,365 FLOP/byte
A softmax at about 1 FLOP/byte
All three speed up by the same 2x
explain: Doubling the flat roof only raises kernels to the right of the old ridge. The GEMV and softmax sit on the sloped bandwidth line, which did not move, so they gain nothing. Only the high intensity GEMM can climb to the new, higher roof.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
question: Your service map has no edge between cart and catalog, yet during an incident both are anomalous and both are on the frontier. What is the most likely explanation worth checking first?
options: A hidden shared dependency (same hosts, same cache, same config push) that is not drawn in the map
Two independent faults at the same moment
The frontier rule does not apply to services with multiple callers
Granger causality between the two metric streams
explain: Two simultaneous frontier nodes usually mean one missing edge, not two faults. Shared infrastructure is the common culprit, and checking it is cheap: look for a resource, host set, or recent change the two have in common. Two genuinely independent faults do happen, but they are the less likely hypothesis, and the troubleshooting chapter's advice applies: when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
question: Why do D1 and D3 tie exactly in the toy example?
options: Rounding to two decimals hides the difference
RRF gives every document that appears in two lists the same score
Their rank pairs (1, 3) and (3, 1) contain the same ranks, and RRF sums the same terms in a different order
Both have the same BM25 score
explain: RRF depends only on the multiset of a document's ranks: the ranks it received, counted with repeats, ignoring which list gave which. 1/61 + 1/63 equals 1/63 + 1/61. D2 is also in two lists but with ranks (2, 5), so it scores lower: two-list documents are not all equal.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: You are writing a Rust driver and need a C function from a subsystem that has no Rust abstraction yet. What does kernel policy expect?
options: Call it through `bindings::` inside an `unsafe` block in the driver, with a SAFETY comment
Add (or extend) a safe abstraction for it in the subsystem's Rust code, and use that from the driver
Rewrite the C function in Rust inside the driver so no FFI is needed
Use `extern "C"` to declare the function by hand in the driver
explain: The general-information doc says leaf modules such as drivers should not use the C bindings directly; subsystems provide as-safe-as-possible abstractions. Declaring the symbol yourself is the same forbidden shortcut with less checking. Duplicating the C logic would create a second implementation to maintain.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
question: A callback receives `t: &Task`. You want a work item to log that task's pid a few seconds later. What do you store in the work item?
options: `ARef::from(t)`: it takes a reference with get_task_struct and drops it with put_task_struct when the work item is dropped
`t` itself, as a `&'static Task` obtained with `core::mem::transmute`
`Arc::new(t)`, which shares the task between the callback and the work item
A bitwise copy of the C `task_struct`
explain: Only the ARef owns an increment of the task's real count. The transmuted reference compiles but nothing keeps the task alive: a use-after-free waiting to happen. `Arc::new(t)` would allocate a new object holding a borrowed `&Task` whose lifetime still ends with the callback, so it does not extend anything. Copying a task_struct copies pointers it does not own.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: Code under review creates `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` once to read and validate a header, then creates a second `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` to read the whole request and use it. What is the problem?
options: It is a double fetch: user memory can change between the two readers, so the validated header is not the one being used
Nothing: `copy_from_user` re-validates the data on every call
It cannot compile, because a `UserSlice` can only be created once per address
The second reader starts where the first one stopped, so it misses the header
explain: Each reader consumes its own UserSlice and advances independently, so the second one starts at the beginning again. `copy_from_user` checks the *address range*, not the contents. The uaccess.rs docs show exactly this pattern labelled as a TOCTOU bug and advise one UserSlice per user memory block.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
